extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants evaluating U.S. §101 subject-matter eligibility (abstract ideas)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the USPTO 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance / Alice two-step framework to determine whether claims are directed to abstract ideas and, if so, whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' (an inventive concept). Uses illustrative examples from Federal Circuit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory Category (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category of invention (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites a process (series of acts), machine (device or set of devices), manufacture, or composition of matter, Step 1 is satisfied (Step 1: YES). Examples: method claims (process), system claims (machine), non-transitory computer-readable medium (manufacture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — Directed to a Judicial Exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is "directed to" a judicial exception (e.g., abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the claim recites concepts similar to those courts have found abstract — e.g., mathematical relationships/algorithms, fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, or an idea standing alone. If no judicial exception is present, the claim is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Abstract-Idea Categories (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories of concepts the Office treats as judicial exceptions: mathematical concepts, fundamental economic practices, methods of organizing human activity, and stand-alone ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedents and examples to map claim language to these categories (e.g., mathematical operations like generating a mask; business practices; data collection/organization concepts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Abstract Idea by Claim Language and Comparable Precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting, an examiner should point to the claim language that describes the abstract idea and explain similarity to court-found abstract concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., explain how a claim describing inventory management is similar to prior abstract-data-collection/management cases (Content Extraction, TLI Communications, Electric Power Group). Provide reasons showing the claim's recited information and operations embody an abstract concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Additional Elements Must Amount to 'Significantly More' (Inventive Concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception, analyze whether any element or combination of elements adds significantly more such that the claim as a whole is patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether limitations (individually or as an ordered combination) provide a meaningful technological improvement beyond the abstract idea. Positive indicators include improvements in the functioning of the computer itself or improvements to another technological field. Negative indicators include mere use of generic computer components to perform conventional functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Computer Components at High Level Do Not Confer Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting well‑understood, routine, conventional computer components (e.g., processor, memory, general-purpose CPU) at a high level of generality does not transform an abstract idea into patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simply adding 'a processor' and 'memory' that perform basic storage and computation is insufficient (mere computer implementation). The Office repeatedly treats such recitals as conventional unless they impose meaningful limits or improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in Computer Functioning or Other Technology Supports 'Significantly More'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements that show an improvement to computer technology itself or an improvement to another technical field can constitute significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a halftoning method that uses a 'blue noise' mask requiring less memory and faster computation (improved functioning) or a GPS solution that increases signal-acquisition sensitivity (improvement to positioning technology) support eligibility (Step 2B: YES).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims 'Rooted in Computer Technology' vs. 'Apply Abstract Idea on the Internet'
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish claims that are necessarily rooted in computer/network technology to solve a problem arising in that realm from claims that merely apply an abstract idea 'on the Internet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely stating 'apply the abstract idea on the Internet' is insufficient. When the claimed limitations are necessarily rooted in computer technology and address an Internet-centric technical problem (e.g., constructing composite web pages to retain visitors), they may amount to significantly more (per DDR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical/Technical Limitation Examples That Can Negate Abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific technical recitations tied to physical/technical structure or operations can show the claim is not directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., reciting the physical isolation of data in a quarantine memory sector and routines that parse and extract flagged bytes (as in the malicious-code removal example) was analyzed as not describing an abstract concept because it is inextricably tied to computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and Manipulation of Particular Information Alone Is Abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely select, manipulate, store, or organize particular information are likely to be considered abstract absent meaningful technological limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite cases where choosing particular data fields and storing/associating them (e.g., adding classification/location data to inventory records) was deemed an abstract data‑collection and management concept. Such recitations, plus generic computer use, typically fail Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Elements Individually and in Ordered Combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether individual claim elements or their ordered combination provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if individual elements are conventional, their particular combination may provide a technological improvement or meaningful limitation (and thus amount to significantly more). The examiner should explain why the combination is meaningful or why it remains conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Remarks / Rejection Drafting Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a rejection, explain (1) which abstract idea is identified and where in the claim it appears, and (2) why additional elements are only conventional computer components or generic steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide analysis comparing claim language to relevant Federal Circuit precedent and explain whether claim elements, alone or in combination, supply any technical improvement or meaningful limits that would convert the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not All Internet-Centric Claims Are Eligible — Must Show More Than Internet Implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims addressing Internet problems are not per se eligible; they must recite additional limitations that are more than simply performing a known business practice on the Internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DDR as guidance: eligibility arose because the claim stored 'visually perceptible elements' and automatically generated composite pages to solve a problem particular to the Internet; the limitations were more than 'apply on the Internet.' Examiners should explain why similar Internet‑centric claims either do or do not amount to significantly more.
